To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a number of thiol radiological protection compounds were tested for inhibition of oxidation of α-keto-glutarate by rat liver homogenates, that in general a correlation exists between inhibition and radiological protection, that inhibition involves oxidation of thiols, and that disulfides are more potent than thiols.
the ability of thiols and disulfides to protect cells from the damaging effects of radiation is correlated with their ability to inhibit mitochondrial oxidation of α-keto acids.
the radioprotection of thiol radiomodulators is not due to their ability to inhibit mitochondrial respiration, but rather to their ability to form mixed disulfides with the protein sulfhydryl groups.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism of radioprotection of normal tissues by thiol compounds, particularly the disulfides, and with the effect of these compounds on the respiration and phosphorylation of mitochondria.
the development of an enzymatic test for thiol radioprotection, and with the use of this test to evaluate the radioprotection of a number of thiol compounds.
the development of new methods for the study of the mechanism of action of radioprotective agents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the inhibition of α-ketoglutate oxidation by thiol and disuffide compounds is related to the ability of these compounds to protect against ionizing radiation.
the radioprotecting action of the thiols is related to a mixed disulfide formation with a critical enzyme, which is inhibited by the disulfides and which is not involved in oxidative phosphorylation.

the radioprotector compounds tested are effective in inhibiting mitochondrial respiration, and that this inhibition is probably due to the oxidation of the thio groups to mixed disulfides, with subsequent inhibition of α-ketoglutamate oxidation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the thiol radioprotection is related to a decrease in the rate of oxidation of the thiolester of glutathione.
the thiol radioprotection is a function of the ability of the compound to form a mixed disulfide with the enzyme glutathione reductase.
a thiol compound, to be radioprotective, must be able to form a mixed disulfide with glutathione, and that this mixed disulfide should not interfere with mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the disulfide form of these compounds are better radioprotectors, but the thiol form are more readily available in cells.
we can now use a simple in vitro test to screen potential radioprotectants and that this test is more reliable than the traditional in vivo test.
the disulfides are more potent than the corresponding thiols, which is consistent with the mixed disulfides theory of Eldjarrn and Pihl.
